questions.problem_before:
If 
$ka≡kb\,(\text{mod}\,8)$
is equivalent to
$a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,8),$
which of the following could be the value of $k?$

I. $k=8$

II. $k=-12$

III. $k=-15$
questions.problem_after:
If 
$ka≡kb\,(\text{mod}\,8)$
is equivalent to
$a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,8),$
which of the following could be the value of $k?$

I. $k=8$

II. $k=-12$

III. $k=-15$

Select all that apply.
questions.worked_solution:
The division property of modular arithmetic states that

$$
ka≡kb\,(\text{mod}\,n)\,⟺\,a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)
$$

provided that $k$ and $n$ are coprime. In other words, we require $\text{gcd}(k,n)=1.$

In this case, the modulus $n=8.$ Let's consider each value of $k$ in turn.

- If $k=8,$ then $\text{gcd}(k,n)=\text{gcd}(8,8)=8\ne 1.$ Therefore, our equivalence is *not* valid for $k=8.$

- If $k=-12,$ then $\text{gcd}(k,n)=\text{gcd}(-12,8)=4\ne 1.$ Therefore, our equivalence is *not* valid for $k=-12.$

- If $k=-15,$ then $\text{gcd}(k,n)=\text{gcd}(-15,8)=1.$ Therefore, our equivalence is valid for $k=-15.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem_before:
$$
{u}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$
- ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthogonal
- ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal
questions.problem_after:
$$
{u}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$
- **II.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthogonal
- **III.** ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=12-12=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})$ is not a unit vector since

$$
‖Q({u}_{1})‖=‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-6)^{2}}\ne 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

choice_mapping.old_value: None of the statements are true.

questions.problem_before:
Consider the following predicates.

$\,$ $A(x):$ $x\ge 2.$ $\,$ $B(x):$ $-x\le -2.$

Which of the following is equivalent to the biconditional predicate $A(x)⇔B(x)?$

- If $x\ge 2$ then $-x\le -2,$ and if $-x\le -2$ then $x\ge 2.$
- $x\ge 2$ is equivalent to $-x\le -2.$
- If $x\ge 2$ then $-x\le -2,$ or if $-x\le -2$ then $x\ge 2.$
questions.problem_after:
Consider the following predicates.

$\,$ $A(x):$ $x\ge 2.$ $\,$ $B(x):$ $-x\le -2.$

Which of the following is equivalent to the biconditional predicate $A(x)⇔B(x)?$
- **I.** If $x\ge 2$ then $-x\le -2,$ and if $-x\le -2$ then $x\ge 2.$
- **II.** $x\ge 2$ is equivalent to $-x\le -2.$
- **III.** If $x\ge 2$ then $-x\le -2,$ or if $-x\le -2$ then $x\ge 2.$

Select all that apply.
questions.worked_solution:
A biconditional expression $P⇔Q≡(P⇒Q)∧(Q⇒P)$ can be read as shown below:

- $P$ if and only if $Q$

- $P$ is equivalent to $Q$

- If $P$ then $Q,$ and if $Q$ then $P$

So, $A⇔B$ translates into the following sentences:

- $x\ge 2$ if and only if $-x\le -2.$

- $x\ge 2$ is equivalent to $-x\le -2.$

- If $x\ge 2$ then $-x\le -2,$ and if $-x\le -2$ then $x\ge 2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.worked_solution:
A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is 

- *reflexive* if $(x,x)\in R$ for all $x\in A,$

- *irreflexive* if $(x,x)\notin R$ for all $x\in A.$

If some pairs of the form $(x,x)$ belong to a relation and others do not, then the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

- Relation $R$ is neither reflexive nor irreflexive. Notice that 

- $(1,1)\notin R$ since $1≢2(1)\,(\text{mod}\,7),$ while

- $(7,7)\in R$ since $7≡2(7)\,(\text{mod}\,7).$

- Relation $S$ is reflexive. Indeed, $(x,x)\in S$ for all $x\in Z.$ Notice that 

$$
x≡x\,(\text{mod}\,9)
$$

for any $x\in Z.$

- Relation $T$ is irreflexive. Indeed, $(x,x)\notin T$ for all $x\in Z.$ Notice that 

$$
x≢x+2\,(\text{mod}\,6)
$$

for any $x\in Z.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$S$ only."

A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is 

- *reflexive* if $(x,x)\in R$ for all $x\in A,$

- *irreflexive* if $(x,x)\notin R$ for all $x\in A.$

If some pairs of the form $(x,x)$ belong to a relation and others do not, then the relation is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.

Since $R$ must be irreflexive, we require 

$$
(1,1)\notin R,\,(2,2)\notin R,\,(3,3)\notin R.
$$

These ordered pairs correspond to the diagonal points on the plots, as shown below:

![](images/b6/b63d99459e8271e70ec36fd417d67565f3d5e77316815d49c235468e174aa1e9.png)

 

A plot corresponding to an irreflexive relation must not contain diagonal points. Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem_before:
Given the matrices

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 7 & 6\end{aligned}]\,Y=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]\,u=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 8\end{aligned}]
$$

 in which of the following expressions is the Hadamard product well-defined?

- $YX⊙Y\,\text{diag}(u)$
- $X⊙Yu$
- $Y\,\text{diag}(u)⊙YX{X}^{T}$

*Hint: Here, $\text{diag}(v)$ is a diagonal matrix with the entries of $v$ on the diagonal.*
questions.problem_after:
Given the matrices

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 7 & 6\end{aligned}]\,Y=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]\,u=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 8\end{aligned}]
$$

 in which of the following expressions is the Hadamard product well-defined?
- **I.** $YX⊙Y\,\text{diag}(u)$
- **II.** $X⊙Yu$
- **III.** $Y\,\text{diag}(u)⊙YX{X}^{T}$

*Hint: Here, $\text{diag}(v)$ is a diagonal matrix with the entries of $v$ on the diagonal.*

Select all that apply.
questions.worked_solution:
The Hadamard product of two matrices (or vectors) is only defined if they have the same dimensions.

First, notice that $X$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix, $Y$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix, and $u$ is a $3\times 1$ column vector.

Now, let's consider each expression in turn:

- The dimensions of $YX$ are $2\times 2,$ and the dimensions of $Y\,\text{diag}(u)$ are $2\times 3.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression I is *not* well-defined.

- The dimensions of $X$ are $3\times 2,$ and the dimensions of $Yu$ are $2\times 1.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression II is *not* well-defined.

- The dimensions of $Y\,\text{diag}(u)$ are $2\times 3,$ and the dimensions of $YX{X}^{T}$ are $2\times 3.$ Hence, the Hadamard product in expression III is well-defined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

questions.problem_before:
Which of the following relations are symmetric? 

- $x\,R\,y$ if and only if $x≡y\,(\text{mod}\,3),$ defined on $Z$

- $x\,S\,y$ if and only if $x+y=0,$ defined on $R$

- $X\,T\,Y$ if and only if $|X|=|Y|,$ defined on $P(N)$
questions.problem_after:
Which of the following relations are symmetric?

Select all that apply.

- **R.** $x\,R\,y$ if and only if $x≡y\,(\text{mod}\,3),$ defined on $Z$

- **S.** $x\,S\,y$ if and only if $x+y=0,$ defined on $R$

- **T.** $X\,T\,Y$ if and only if $|X|=|Y|,$ defined on $P(N)$
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall the following definitions:

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *symmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,⟹\,(y,x)\in R.
$$

In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *antisymmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

- Relation $R$ is symmetric. Indeed, if $(x,y)\in R$ then $(y,x)\in R.$ Notice that 

$$
x≡y\,(\text{mod}\,3)\,⟹\,y≡x\,(\text{mod}\,3)
$$

for all $x,y\in Z.$

- Relation $S$ is symmetric. Indeed, if $(x,y)\in S$ then $(y,x)\in S.$ Notice that 

$$
x+y=0\,⟹\,y+x=0
$$

for all $x,y\in R.$

- Relation $T$ is symmetric. Indeed, if $(X,Y)\in T$ then $(Y,X)\in T.$ Notice that 

$$
|X|=|Y|\,⟹\,|Y|=|X|
$$

for all $X,Y\in P(N).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$R$, $S,$ and $T.$"

$$
(x,y)\in R\,⟹\,(y,x)\in R.
$$

In terms of a digraph, if we have an arrow $x\to y,$ then the arrow $y\to x$ must be in the digraph too.

$$
(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

So, only one of the arrows, either $x\to y$ or $y\to x,$ can be in the digraph of an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows loops.

With that in mind, let's examine our digraphs.

- Digraph I represents an antisymmetric relation since for all possible $x$ and $y$ with $x\ne y,$ *at most one* of the arrows (either $x\to y$ or $y\to x,$ but not both) belongs to the digraph.

- Digraph II represents a symmetric relation since for every arrow $x\to y$ belonging to the graph, the corresponding inverse arrow $y\to x$ also belongs to the graph.

- Digraph III represents neither a symmetric nor an antisymmetric relation. It's not symmetric since the arrow $1\to 2$ belongs to the digraph while the arrow $2\to 1$ does not. It is not antisymmetric since, for example, arrows $1\to 3$ and $3\to 1$ belong to the digraph.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem_after:
Let $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T$ and ${u}_{1},{u}_{2}\in {R}^{3}.$  Consider the following statement:

*If ${u}_{1}-{u}_{2}\ne 0$ and $T({u}_{1})-T({u}_{2})=0,$ then $\text{__________}.$*

Which of the following can be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?
- **I.** $\text{Ker}(T)={0}$
- **II.** $\text{rank}(T)\ne 3$
- **III.** $T$ is invertible

Select all that apply.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since $T$ is a linear transformation and $T({u}_{1})-T({u}_{2})=0,$ we have $T({u}_{1}-{u}_{2})=0.$ So ${u}_{1}-{u}_{2}\in \text{Ker}(T)$ and ${u}_{1}-{u}_{2}\ne 0.$ Therefore, we must have $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement II is true. Since $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}$, then $\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)\ne 3.$

- Statement III is false. According to the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{rank}(T)\ne 3,$ the transformation $T$ can't be invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

- **II.** ${R}_{2}={A}^{2}$
- **III.** ${R}_{3}={(5,5)}$
- **IV.** ${R}_{4}={(5,1),(7,3)}$

Select all that apply.
questions.worked_solution:
A binary relation $R$ defined on a set $A$ is *transitive* if, for all $x,y,z\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,z)\in R\,⟹\,(x,z)\in R.
$$

In other words, if the pairs $(x,y)$ and $(y,z)$ belong to a transitive relation, then the pair $(x,z)$ should also be in the relation.

It's sufficient to check all the "linked" pairs of the form $(x,y)$ with $x\ne y$ and $(y,z)$ with $y\ne z:$

Moreover, we recall the following:

- The universal relation $R={A}^{2}$ is transitive since it includes all possible ordered pairs.

- The empty relation $R=∅$ is vacuously transitive since the antecedent in the implication is always false, and therefore the implication is always true.

- A relation containing no "linked" pairs is always transitive.

- A relation containing only reflexive pairs is always transitive.

With that in mind, let's examine our relations:

- ${R}_{1}$ is transitive since it's the empty relation. $\,\,✓$

- ${R}_{2}$ is transitive since it's the universal relation. $\,\,✓$

- ${R}_{3}$ is transitive since it contains only reflexive pairs.  $\,\,✓$

- ${R}_{4}$ is transitive since it contains no "linked" pairs.  $\,\,✓$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, III, and IV."

questions.problem_before:
Which of the following relations are transitive? 

- $x\,R\,y$ if and only if $x∣y,$ defined on $Z$

- $x\,S\,y$ if and only if $x+y<4,$ defined on $R$

- $x\,T\,y$ if and only if $x≡y\,(\text{mod}\,4),$ defined on $Z$
questions.problem_after:
Which of the following relations are transitive?

Select all that apply.

- **R.** $x\,R\,y$ if and only if $x∣y,$ defined on $Z$

- **S.** $x\,S\,y$ if and only if $x+y<4,$ defined on $R$

- **T.** $x\,T\,y$ if and only if $x≡y\,(\text{mod}\,4),$ defined on $Z$
questions.worked_solution:
A binary relation $R$ defined on a set $A$ is *transitive* if, for all $x,y,z\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,z)\in R\,⟹\,(x,z)\in R.
$$

In other words, if the pairs $(x,y)$ and $(y,z)$ belong to a transitive relation, then the pair $(x,z)$ should also be in the relation.

It's sufficient to check all the "linked" pairs of the form $(x,y)$ with $x\ne y$ and $(y,z)$ with $y\ne z.$

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

- Relation $R$ is transitive. Indeed, if $(x,y)\in R$ and $(y,x)\in R,$ then $(x,z)\in R.$ Notice that 

$$
x∣y\,\text{and}\,y∣z\,⟹\,x∣z
$$

for all $x,y,z\in Z.$

- Relation $S$ is not transitive. Notice that 

- $(1,-4)\in S$ since $1+(-4)=-3<4,$ and

- $(-4,5)\in S$ since $-4+5=1<4,$ but

- $(1,5)\notin S$ since $1+5=6≮4.$

- Relation $T$ is transitive. Indeed, if $(x,y)\in T$ and $(y,x)\in T,$ then $(x,z)\in T.$ Notice that 

$$
x≡y\,(\text{mod}\,4)\,\text{and}\,y≡z\,(\text{mod}\,4)\,⟹\,x≡z\,(\text{mod}\,4)
$$

for all $x,y,z\in Z.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$R$ and $T$ only."

questions.problem_before:
Given that $-21≡-12\,(\text{mod}\,n),$ which of the following could be the value of $n?$

- $n=3$
- $n=9$
- $n=12$
questions.problem_after:
Given that $-21≡-12\,(\text{mod}\,n),$ which of the following could be the value of $n?$
- **I.** $n=3$
- **II.** $n=9$
- **III.** $n=12$

Select all that apply.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall that 

$$
a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\,⟺\,n∣(a-b).
$$

So, $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $n$ if and only if $(a-b)$ is divisible by $n$ (there is no remainder).

We have $a-b=-21-(-12)=-9.$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Note that $3∣(-9)$ because $(-9)÷3=-3,$ and there is no remainder. Therefore, the statement is true when $n=3.$

- Note that $9∣(-9)$ because $(-9)÷9=-1,$ and there is no remainder. Therefore, the statement is true when $n=9.$

- Note that $12∤(-9).$ Therefore, the statement is false when $n=12.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem_before:
A triangle $S$ has vertices at  $(-1,3),(-2,2),(1,-4).$ Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of ${S}^{′},$ the image of $S$ under the **clockwise** rotation ${R}_{-{90}^{∘}}$ by an angle of ${90}^{∘}$ about the origin?

- $(3,1)$
- $(2,-2)$
- $(-4,-1)$
questions.problem_after:
A triangle $S$ has vertices at  $(-1,3),(-2,2),(1,-4).$ Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of ${S}^{′},$ the image of $S$ under the **clockwise** rotation ${R}_{-{90}^{∘}}$ by an angle of ${90}^{∘}$ about the origin?
- **I.** $(3,1)$
- **II.** $(2,-2)$
- **III.** $(-4,-1)$

Select all that apply.
questions.worked_solution:
The clockwise rotation ${R}_{-{90}^{∘}}$ by an angle of ${90}^{∘}$ is the same as counterclockwise rotation by an angle of ${270}^{∘}.$ It's given by the matrix

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the image of $S$ under the action of ${R}_{-{90}^{∘}},$ we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under ${R}_{-{90}^{∘}}$ by calculating the matrix product $RX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}RX & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -4 \\ 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of ${S}^{′}$ are $(3,1),(2,2),(-4,-1).$

So, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem_before:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $f:R\to R$ which is given by $f(x)={3}^{x}+1?$

I. The range of $f$ is $(1,\infty )$

II. $∀\,y\in (1,\infty ),$ $∃\,x\in R$ such that $f(x)=y$

III. $f$ maps $R$ **into** $R$
questions.problem_after:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $f:R\to R$ which is given by $f(x)={3}^{x}+1?$

I. The range of $f$ is $(1,\infty )$

II. $∀\,y\in (1,\infty ),$ $∃\,x\in R$ such that $f(x)=y$

III. $f$ maps $R$ **into** $R$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we graph the function.

![](images/0c/0cb3e23cecdbd82803f5757827f21a424672bdde6da03782ca995d23e1c4d7b4.png)

Recall that $f:X\to Y$ is an *into* function if it is not a surjection. In other words, there exists an element $y$ in $Y$ such that it has no preimage in $X:$ 

$f:X\to Y$ is an into function if $∃\,y\in Y$ such that $∀\,x\in X,$ we have $f(x)\ne y.$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. From the graph, the function takes all $y$-values greater than $y=1$, excluding $y=1$ itself. So the range of the function is indeed $(1,\infty ).$

- Statement II is true. Since the range of the function is $(1,\infty )$, then for all $y$ contained within $(1,\infty ),$ there exists some $x$ contained within $R$ such that $f(x)=y.$

- Statement III is true. As we can see from the range, there is no real number $x$ such that $f(x)=0\in R.$ So, $f$ maps $R$ *into* $R.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.problem_before:
Which of the following sets are infinite?

I. $A={n\in Z\,:\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi )=0}$

II. $B={q\in Q\,:\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2q\pi )=0}$

III. $C={x\in R\,:\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\pi )=0}$
questions.problem_after:
Which of the following sets are infinite?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A={n\in Z\,:\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi )=0}$

- **II.** $B={q\in Q\,:\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2q\pi )=0}$

- **III.** $C={x\in R\,:\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\pi )=0}$
questions.worked_solution:
The cardinality of a finite set is the number of elements contained within it. A set is infinite if it has infinitely many elements.

We start by finding the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\pi )=0$ for $x\in R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\pi  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+m\pi  \\ x & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{m}{2},\,m\in Z\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets:

- The set $A$ is finite. There are no values of $m\in Z$ such that $\frac{1}{4}+\frac{m}{2}\in Z.$ Therefore,

$$
A={}.
$$

Consequently, $|A|=0,$ which is finite.

- The set $B$ is infinite. Listing the elements of $B$ for different values of $m,$ we have

$$
B={…,-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4},…}.
$$

- The set $C$ is infinite. Since $B$ is infinite, and $B⊆C,$ it follows that $C$ is infinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$B$ and $C$ only."

I. $A={{f}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}({e}^{1-2x})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$

II. $B={{g}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(3{e}^{x})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$

questions.problem_after:
Which of the following sets are infinite?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A={{f}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}({e}^{1-2x})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$

- **II.** $B={{g}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(3{e}^{x})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$

- **III.** $C={{h}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(4{e}^{-x})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$
questions.worked_solution:
The cardinality of a finite set is the number of elements contained within it. A set is infinite if it has infinitely many elements.

- The set $A$ is infinite. Listing the first few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{(0)}(x) & ={e}^{1-2x} \\ {f}^{(1)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{1-2x})=-2{e}^{1-2x} \\ {f}^{(2)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2{e}^{1-2x})=4{e}^{1-2x} \\ {f}^{(3)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{e}^{1-2x})=-8{e}^{1-2x} \\ ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we can write our set as follows:

$$
A={{e}^{1-2x},-2{e}^{1-2x},4{e}^{1-2x},-8{e}^{1-2x},…}
$$

Consequently, $A$ is infinite.

- The set $B$ is finite. Listing the first few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{(0)}(x) & =3{e}^{x} \\ {g}^{(1)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{e}^{x})=3{e}^{x} \\ {g}^{(2)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{e}^{x})=3{e}^{x} \\ {g}^{(3)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{e}^{x})=3{e}^{x} \\ ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $B$ contains only one element:

$$
B={3{e}^{x}}
$$

Consequently, $|B|=1,$ which is finite.

- The set $C$ is finite. Listing the first few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{(0)}(x) & =4{e}^{-x} \\ {h}^{(1)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{e}^{-x})=-4{e}^{-x} \\ {h}^{(2)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4{e}^{-x})=4{e}^{-x} \\ {h}^{(3)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{e}^{-x})=-4{e}^{-x} \\ ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $C$ contains only two elements:

$$
C={4{e}^{-x},-4{e}^{-x}}.
$$

Consequently, $|C|=2,$ which is finite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$A$ only."

questions.problem_after:
Which of the following sets are infinite?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A={n\in Z\,:\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi }{2})=0}$

- **II.** $B={q\in Q\,:\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{q\pi }{2})=0}$

- **III.** $C={x\in R\,:\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x\pi }{2})=0}$
questions.worked_solution:
The cardinality of a finite set is the number of elements contained within it. A set is infinite if it has infinitely many elements.

We start by finding the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x\pi }{2})=0$ for $x\in R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x\pi }{2} & =m\pi  \\ x & =2m,\,m\in Z\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets:

- The set $A$ is infinite. Listing the elements of $B$ for different values of $m,$ we have

$$
A={…,-2,0,2,4,…}.
$$

- The set $B$ is infinite. Since $A$ is infinite, and $A⊆B,$ it follows that $B$ is infinite.

- The set $C$ is infinite. Since $B$ is infinite, and $B⊆C,$ it follows that $C$ is infinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$A,$ $B,$ and $C.$"

kps.title: Sets Defined Using Derivatives

atomic_options.label: I
atomic_options.proof: On x>0 the function equals x^(2/5). The nth derivative is c_n x^(2/5-n), with c_n!=0 and distinct powers; hence infinitely many functions.

atomic_options.label: II
atomic_options.proof: On x>0 the nth derivative of -x^(1/2) is c_n x^(1/2-n), with c_n!=0 and distinct powers.

atomic_options.label: III
atomic_options.proof: The nth derivative of x^(-2) is (-1)^n(n+1)!x^(-n-2), with distinct powers and nonzero coefficients.

questions.problem_before:
Which of the following sets are infinite?

I. $A={{f}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$

II. $B={{g}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(-\sqrt{x})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$

III. $C={{h}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$
questions.problem_after:
Which of the following sets are infinite?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A={{f}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$

- **II.** $B={{g}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(-\sqrt{x})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$

- **III.** $C={{h}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$
questions.worked_solution:
The cardinality of a finite set is the number of elements contained within it. A set is infinite if it has infinitely many elements.

- The set $A$ is infinite. Listing the first few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{(0)}(x) & =\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{(1)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}})=\frac{2}{5\sqrt[5]{{x}^{3}}} \\ {f}^{(2)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{5\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}})=-\frac{6}{25\sqrt[5]{{x}^{8}}} \\ ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we can write our set as follows:

$$
A={\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}},\frac{2}{5\sqrt[5]{{x}^{3}}},-\frac{6}{25\sqrt[5]{{x}^{8}}},…}
$$

Consequently, $A$ is infinite.

- The set $B$ is also infinite. Similar to the previous case, listing the first few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{(0)}(x) & =-\sqrt{x} \\ {g}^{(1)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\sqrt{x})=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ {g}^{(2)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}} \\  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we can write our set as follows:

$$
B={-\sqrt{x},-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}},\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}},…}
$$

Consequently, $B$ is infinite.

- The set $C$ is also infinite. Listing a few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{(0)}(x) & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {h}^{(1)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})=-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}} \\ {h}^{(2)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})=\frac{6}{{x}^{4}} \\  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we can write our set as follows:

$$
C={\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}},\frac{6}{{x}^{4}},…}
$$

Consequently, $C$ is infinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$A,$ $B,$ and $C.$"
